# Zero Day

## Chapter 14: Day Ninety

The email sat in Maya Okafor's drafts folder for three days before she sent it.

Not because she was unsure of the facts. The facts were airtight—forty-one pages of technical documentation, proof-of-concept code redacted to uselessness, a remediation timeline, and a disclosure history stretching back exactly ninety days to the first contact on March 12th. She'd built the file the way she built everything: methodically, obsessively, with the kind of care that came from knowing one mistake could end a career.

She hesitated because she knew what happened next.

*Once you send this, you can't take it back.*

She looked at the clock. 11:47 PM. Outside her apartment window, Portland glittered in that exhausted, late-night way, and somewhere across the Pacific, in a data center outside Taipei, the vulnerability was still there. Still live. Still exploitable in roughly 2.3 million industrial control systems—water treatment plants, hospital HVAC networks, three national power grids she knew of and probably two she didn't.

Ninety days. That was the industry standard, the coordinated disclosure window she'd insisted on when Meridian Systems' security team first responded to her report. *We need time to patch*, they'd said. *Our customers run critical infrastructure. You can't just drop this on them.*

Fine. Ninety days. She'd agreed, and she'd kept her end of it. She'd answered their questions. She'd helped their engineers reproduce the flaw—a race condition in the authentication handshake that let an attacker replay session tokens indefinitely, walking through the front door of systems that were supposed to be sealed. She'd even reviewed their patch, back in April, and told them it was incomplete. They'd shipped it anyway.

That was the part that kept her up at night. Not the disclosure. The patch.

She pulled up the thread again, scrolling to Meridian's last message, dated six days ago:

*Ms. Okafor — Meridian appreciates your continued cooperation. Our engineering team has confirmed the remediation is complete and deployed to all affected endpoints. We consider this matter closed and trust you will honor the terms of our agreement.*

*We consider this matter closed.*

She'd spent the last six days doing what she did best: proving them wrong. Quietly. From a VM in her closet that had never touched Meridian's network. The incomplete patch could be bypassed with a twelve-line script. She'd written it in forty minutes, then spent three days trying to talk herself out of what she already knew.

If she disclosed the original vulnerability without mentioning the broken patch, thousands of admins would apply the fix, check the box, and go back to sleep—while the door stood open.

If she disclosed everything—the flaw, the failed patch, the bypass—Meridian would come after her. Their legal team had already sent one letter, back in May, when she'd presented a sanitized version of the research at a conference. *Defamation. Trade secret exposure. DMCA violations.* The letter was theater, mostly. But theater with lawyers behind it.

And if she stayed silent?

She thought about the water utility outside Tulsa she'd visited in February, back when she was still mapping the attack surface. A plant operator named Ruiz, sixty years old, three weeks from retirement, who'd shown her the control room with the pride of a man showing off his grandchildren. *Nobody's coming after us,* he'd said. *We're too small. Too boring.*

The replay attack didn't care about boring. It cared about reachable.

Maya opened the disclosure email one more time. She'd rewritten the opening paragraph four times, trying to find the tone that was firm without being inflammatory, factual without being cold. She'd finally settled on the truth, plainly stated:

*This is a coordinated disclosure of CVE-2024-31877, per the 90-day timeline agreed upon on March 12, 2024. Additionally, this disclosure includes a critical finding: the patch released by Meridian Systems on April 28 does not fully remediate the vulnerability. A working bypass exists and is documented in Section 7. I strongly recommend Meridian issue a corrected patch immediately and notify affected customers of the urgency.*

She attached the report. She CC'd CERT/CC, the ICS-CERT coordination center, and—after a long pause—two journalists she trusted, with a note explaining the timeline and offering the full disclosure history for verification. That last part was the insurance policy. If Meridian wanted to make this about her, it would help that the record showed ninety days of good faith, documented to the timestamp.

Her cursor hovered over Send.

Her phone buzzed. Unknown number. A text:

*Maya. It's Daniel Chen, Meridian CSO. Please don't send that email. I know about the bypass. We can fix this quietly. Give me
